title: Seeing Without Understanding: Disentangling Perception, Reasoning, and Simulation in VLM Gameplay
claim: Evaluation decomposes into isolated perception tests plus a graded rule-following suite, so failures can be attributed to specific capabilities.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, left-to-right, rounded headers, nested boxes with a ladder chart
description: The figure has two columns, each with a peach rounded header. The left column, 'Perception Test Suite', is a 2x2 grid of boxes: Density (a chess board), Patch Alignment (a Go board with a red patch grid overlay), Resolution (nested squares marked 512x512 and 1024x1024 with arrows), and Visual Richness (a textured Go board). The right column, 'Rule Following Test Suite', has a tall vertical bar labeled 'Verified Perception'. Next to it are two stacked boxes: Single-State, a chess capture example with a 'Rule Baseline' of no rule vs. with rules, and Multi-States, stacked boards for state tracking. On the far right, a 'Rule Complexity Ladder' shows ascending beige bars from Simple to Complex with a diagonal arrow. Below the bars, a small table lists Predictive (N) and Explicit (N+1) modes. Warm beige and peach tones dominate.
caption: Two-Stage Diagnostic Framework. Stage 1 isolates VLM performance on perception accuracy. Stage 2 evaluates rule following via a diagnostic matrix, and a six-level complexity ladder with Explicit and Predictive testing modes for fine-grained capability analysis.
abstract: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel on static visual benchmarks, they consistently underperform in game-based reasoning, yet existing evaluations conflate failures in perception, rule comprehension, and reasoning. We propose a two-stage diagnostic framework that decomposes VLM performance into testable components: controlled perception tests isolating visual encoding, and a diagnostic matrix with a six-level rule complexity ladder evaluated in both explicit verification and predictive simulation modes. Experimenting with six state-of-the-art VLMs reveals three failure patterns: (1) coordinated spatial drift, where off-by-one localization errors among adjacent pieces share the same shift direction at $1.5$-$1.9\times$ the rate expected under spatial independence; (2) perception-reasoning dissociation, where models correctly verify board states but fail to apply rules—at complex constraint levels, perception remains relatively stable while reasoning accuracy plummets, with even the best-performing model capped at $75\%$; and (3) a simulation gap, with performance dropping by up to $27$ points when predicting future states versus verifying observed outcomes. These limitations persist across model scales and are not resolved by scaling, text-only input, or structured prompting. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chillibeaver/PRS-Diag.
